claim: PKD2 (polycystin-2, TRPP1) is a TRP polycystin channel expressed in endothelial cells.
source: PKD2 (polycystin-2, TRPP1), a TRP polycystin channel, is expressed in endothelial cells (ECs), but its physiological functions in this cell type are unclear.
evidence: The statement is presented as established fact in the abstract, supported by the subsequent experimental demonstration of PKD2 protein in endothelial cells.

claim: A broad range of intravascular flow rates stimulate EC PKD2 channels, producing vasodilation.
source: Data show that a broad range of intravascular flow rates stimulate EC PKD2 channels, producing vasodilation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing flow-mediated vasodilation across shear stress ranges of 3-35 dyn/cm2 in pressurized arteries.

claim: Flow-mediated PKD2 channel activation leads to calcium influx that activates SK/IK channels in ECs.
source: Flow-mediated PKD2 channel activation leads to calcium influx that activates SK/IK channels and eNOS serine 1176 phosphorylation in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data showing flow-induced Ca2+-dependent currents and pharmacological experiments with SK/IK channel blockers.

claim: Flow-mediated PKD2 channel activation leads to eNOS serine 1176 phosphorylation in ECs.
source: Flow-mediated PKD2 channel activation leads to calcium influx that activates SK/IK channels and eNOS serine 1176 phosphorylation in ECs.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased p-eNOS (S1176) protein in response to flow in Pkd2fl/fl but not Pkd2 ecKO arteries.

claim: PKD2-mediated signaling mechanisms produce arterial hyperpolarization and vasodilation.
source: These signaling mechanisms produce arterial hyperpolarization and vasodilation.
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements showing flow-induced hyperpolarization in Pkd2fl/fl but not Pkd2 ecKO arteries.

claim: EC PKD2 channels do not contribute to acetylcholine-induced vasodilation.
source: In contrast, EC PKD2 channels do not contribute to acetylcholine-induced vasodilation, suggesting stimulus-specific function.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing similar ACh-induced vasodilation in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries.

claim: EC-specific PKD2 knockout elevated blood pressure in mice.
source: EC-specific PKD2 knockout elevated blood pressure in mice without altering cardiac function or kidney anatomy.
evidence: This is supported by telemetry measurements showing increased diastolic and systolic blood pressure in Pkd2 ecKO mice.

claim: EC-specific PKD2 knockout did not alter cardiac function.
source: EC-specific PKD2 knockout elevated blood pressure in mice without altering cardiac function or kidney anatomy.
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data showing similar cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction, and heart rate in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.

claim: EC-specific PKD2 knockout did not alter kidney anatomy.
source: EC-specific PKD2 knockout elevated blood pressure in mice without altering cardiac function or kidney anatomy.
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing similar proximal tubule diameter and glomerular area in kidneys of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.

claim: PKD2 channels are a major component of functional flow sensing in the vasculature.
source: Thus, PKD2 channels are a major component of functional flow sensing in the vasculature.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the collective experimental data showing PKD2's role in flow-mediated vasodilation and blood pressure regulation.

claim: Endothelial cells line the lumen of all blood vessels and regulate multiple functions, including contractility.
source: Endothelial cells line the lumen of all blood vessels and regulate multiple functions, including contractility.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about endothelial cell anatomy and function.

claim: Acetylcholine acts through endothelial cells to control arterial contractility.
source: A wide variety of different stimuli act through endothelial cells to control arterial contractility, including receptor ligands, such as acetylcholine (ACh), and mechanical force, including intravascular flow.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about endothelial cell function.

claim: Intravascular flow acts through endothelial cells to control arterial contractility.
source: A wide variety of different stimuli act through endothelial cells to control arterial contractility, including receptor ligands, such as acetylcholine (ACh), and mechanical force, including intravascular flow.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about endothelial cell function.

claim: Endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility through the production of nitric oxide.
source: Mechanisms by which endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility include the production of diffusible substances, such as nitric oxide (NO) and hydrogen sulfide, and the release of endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors, including potassium (K+) (Vane, 1994; Edwards et al., 1998; Leffler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility through the production of hydrogen sulfide.
source: Mechanisms by which endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility include the production of diffusible substances, such as nitric oxide (NO) and hydrogen sulfide, and the release of endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors, including potassium (K+) (Vane, 1994; Edwards et al., 1998; Leffler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility through the release of endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors, including potassium.
source: Mechanisms by which endothelial cells regulate arterial contractility include the production of diffusible substances, such as nitric oxide (NO) and hydrogen sulfide, and the release of endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors, including potassium (K+) (Vane, 1994; Edwards et al., 1998; Leffler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cells can directly control smooth muscle cell membrane potential to regulate arterial contractility due to the presence of myoendothelial gap junctions.
source: Due to the presence of myoendothelial gap junctions, endothelial cells can also directly control smooth muscle cell membrane potential to regulate arterial contractility (Garland et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cells express several different families of ion channels, including TRP, SK3, and IK proteins.
source: Endothelial cells express several different families of ion channels, including multiple transient receptor potential (TRP), small-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (SK3, KCa2.3) and intermediate-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (IK, KCa3.1) proteins (Jackson, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TRP channels are a family of ~28 proteins subdivided into six different classes.
source: TRP channels are a family of ~28 proteins that are subdivided into six different classes, including polycystin (TRPP), melastatin (TRPM), ankyrin (TRPA), canonical (TRPC) and vanilloid (TRPV) (Earley and Brayden, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Approximately twenty different TRP channels may be expressed in endothelial cells.
source: Studies performed using whole arteries and veins, which contain multiple different cell types, and cultured and non-cultured cells have proposed that approximately twenty different TRP channels may be expressed in endothelial cells (Sullivan and Earley, 2013; Bulley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TRPV4 channels present in endothelial cells regulate the contractility of vasculature, including resistance-size arteries.
source: A significant body of work indicates that TRPV4 channels present in endothelial cells regulate the contractility of vasculature, including resistance-size arteries (Earley et al., 2009; Sonkusare et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2009; Köhler et al., 2006; Marrelli et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cell TRPA1, TRPC3, TRPC4, TRPV1 and TRPV3 channels modulate vascular contractility.
source: Evidence also suggests that endothelial cell TRPA1, TRPC3, TRPC4, TRPV1 and TRPV3 channels modulate vascular contractility (Liu et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2012; Freichel et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2010; Bratz et al., 2008; Earley et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 is encoded by the Pkd2 gene.
source: PKD2, which is also termed Transient Receptor Potential Polycystin 1 (TRPP1), PC-2 and polycystin-2, is encoded by the Pkd2 gene (Mochizuki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PKD2 contains six transmembrane domains, cytoplasmic N and C termini and a characteristic extracellular polycystin domain.
source: PKD2 contains six transmembrane domains, cytoplasmic N and C termini and a characteristic extracellular polycystin domain (Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: PKD2 protein is expressed in endothelium, arterial smooth muscle, renal epithelia, cardiac myocytes and neurons.
source: PKD2 protein is expressed in a wide variety of different cell types, including endothelium, arterial smooth muscle, renal epithelia, cardiac myocytes and neurons, (Bulley et al., 2018; Semmo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mutations in Pkd2 lead to Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD).
source: Mutations in Pkd2 lead to Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide (Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: ADPKD is the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide.
source: Mutations in Pkd2 lead to Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD), the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide (Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A significant proportion of ADPKD patients develop hypertension prior to kidney dysfunction.
source: ADPKD is typically characterized by the growth of renal cysts, although a significant proportion of patients develop hypertension prior to kidney dysfunction, suggesting PKD2 channels perform physiological functions in vascular wall cell types (Torres et al., 2007; Valero et al., 1999; Martinez-Vea et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intravascular pressure activates PKD2 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells of different organs, leading to depolarization, vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic blood pressure.
source: We have previously shown that intravascular pressure and α1-adrenoceptors activate PKD2 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells of different organs, leading to depolarization, vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic blood pressure (Bulley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: α1-adrenoceptors activate PKD2 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells of different organs, leading to depolarization, vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic blood pressure.
source: We have previously shown that intravascular pressure and α1-adrenoceptors activate PKD2 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells of different organs, leading to depolarization, vasoconstriction and an increase in systemic blood pressure (Bulley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: Tamoxifen stimulated Pkd2 recombination in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice.
source: Genomic PCR confirmed that tamoxifen stimulated Pkd2 recombination in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice, but not in arteries of Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tamoxifen did not stimulate Pkd2 recombination in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Genomic PCR confirmed that tamoxifen stimulated Pkd2 recombination in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice, but not in arteries of Pkd2fl/fl mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PKD2 protein in mesenteric arteries of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice was ~ 67.2% of that in tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl controls.
source: PKD2 protein in mesenteric arteries of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice was ~ 67.2% of that in tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl controls (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: SK3, IK, TRPV4, Piezo1, GPR68 and PKD1 proteins were similar in arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice.
source: In contrast, SK3, IK, TRPV4, Piezo1, GPR68 and PKD1 (polycystin-1, PC-1), which can form a complex with PKD2 (Qian et al., 1997; Tsiokas et al., 1997), were similar in arteries of both genotypes (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1a and b.

claim: PKD1 can form a complex with PKD2.
source: In contrast, SK3, IK, TRPV4, Piezo1, GPR68 and PKD1 (polycystin-1, PC-1), which can form a complex with PKD2 (Qian et al., 1997; Tsiokas et al., 1997), were similar in arteries of both genotypes (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 protein was present in endothelial cells of intact arteries from tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Immunofluorescence demonstrated that PKD2 protein was present in endothelial cells of intact arteries from tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl mice, but absent in endothelial cells of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PKD2 protein was absent in endothelial cells of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice.
source: Immunofluorescence demonstrated that PKD2 protein was present in endothelial cells of intact arteries from tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl mice, but absent in endothelial cells of tamoxifen-treated Pkd2fl/fl:Cdh5-creERT2 mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Vasodilation to ACh was similar in control and Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: Vasodilation to ACh, a muscarinic receptor agonist, was similar in control and Pkd2 ecKO arteries, suggesting that endothelial cell PKD2 channels do not contribute to this response (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: Repetitive intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2) stimuli produced sustained, reproducible and fully reversible vasodilation in pressurized (80 mmHg) mesenteric arteries.
source: Repetitive intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2) stimuli produced sustained, reproducible and fully reversible vasodilation in pressurized (80 mmHg) mesenteric arteries (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Mean vasodilation to single on-off flow stimuli in pressurized Pkd2 ecKO arteries were ~35.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: In pressurized Pkd2 ecKO arteries, mean vasodilation to single on-off flow stimuli were ~35.1% of those in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Endothelial cell-denudation abolished vasodilation to both flow and ACh.
source: Endothelial cell-denudation abolished vasodilation to both flow and ACh (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Cumulative increases in flow caused progressive dilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, with a maximum at 27 dyn/cm2.
source: Cumulative increases in flow caused progressive dilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, with a maximum at 27 dyn/cm2 (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Flow-mediated vasodilation was between ~ 45.5% and 60.1% of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries in Pkd2 ecKO arteries, regardless of flow rate.
source: Specifically, flow-mediated vasodilation was between ~ 45.5% and 60.1% of that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, regardless of rate (Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2D and E, Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: An increase in extracellular potassium (60 mm K+) similarly constricted arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: An increase in extracellular potassium (60 mm K+) or intravascular pressure (80 mmHg) similarly constricted arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice, indicating that endothelial cell PKD2 channels or their knockout does not influence depolarization-induced vasoconstriction or myogenic tone, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: An increase in intravascular pressure (80 mmHg) similarly constricted arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: An increase in extracellular potassium (60 mm K+) or intravascular pressure (80 mmHg) similarly constricted arteries of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice, indicating that endothelial cell PKD2 channels or their knockout does not influence depolarization-induced vasoconstriction or myogenic tone, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: Arterial passive diameter was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: Similarly, arterial passive diameter, determined by removal of extracellular Ca2+ from the bath solution, was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E.

claim: At 10 mmHg, the mean membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries were similar at ~ −62.1 and −61.1 mV, respectively.
source: At 10 mmHg, the mean membrane potential of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries were similar at ~ −62.1 and −61.1 mV, respectively (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Increasing intravascular pressure to 80 mmHg similarly depolarized Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries by ~ 19.3 and 17.7 mV, respectively.
source: Increasing intravascular pressure to 80 mmHg similarly depolarized Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO arteries by ~ 19.3 and 17.7 mV, respectively (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Intravascular flow stimulated a mean hyperpolarization of ~ 11 mV in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: Intravascular flow stimulated a mean hyperpolarization of ~ 11 mV in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Flow only hyperpolarized Pkd2 ecKO arteries by ~ 3 mV, or ~ 25.5% of that in controls.
source: In contrast, flow only hyperpolarized Pkd2 ecKO arteries by ~ 3 mV, or ~ 25.5% of that in controls (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by membrane potential measurements shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In a static bath, Pkd2fl/fl endothelial cells generated a mean steady-state inward current of ~−80 pA.
source: In a static bath, Pkd2fl/fl endothelial cells generated a mean steady-state inward current of ~−80 pA (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Flow stimulated an initial, transient peak increase in mean inward current of ~−21 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Flow stimulated an initial, transient peak increase in mean inward current of ~−21 pA that was followed by a sustained reduction in inward current that plateaued at ~−11 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4-C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Flow stimulated a sustained reduction in inward current that plateaued at ~−11 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Flow stimulated an initial, transient peak increase in mean inward current of ~−21 pA that was followed by a sustained reduction in inward current that plateaued at ~−11 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4-C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the continuous presence of flow, the removal of bath Ca2+ increased mean inward current to ~−53 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: In the continuous presence of flow, the removal of bath Ca2+ increased mean inward current to ~−53 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Mean steady-state inward current was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells in a static bath.
source: In a static bath, mean steady-state inward current was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Flow activated a transient peak inward current in Pkd2 ecKO cells that was only ~ 15% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: In contrast, flow activated a transient peak inward current in Pkd2 ecKO cells that was only ~ 15% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The sustained flow-mediated reduction in inward current in Pkd2 ecKO cells was ~ 40% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Similarly, the sustained flow-mediated reduction in inward current in Pkd2 ecKO cells was ~ 40% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Under flow Ca2+ removal increased inward current only ~ 25 pA in Pkd2 ecKO cells, which was ~ 48.8% of the response in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Specifically, under flow Ca2+ removal increased inward current only ~ 25 pA in Pkd2 ecKO cells, which was ~ 48.8% of the response in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Under flow, the co-application of apamin and Tram-34 increased mean inward current by ~ 23.2 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: Under flow, the co-application of apamin and Tram-34, SK and IK channel blockers respectively, increased mean inward current by ~ 23.2 pA in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A,B,D.

claim: The apamin/tram-34-mediated increase in inward current under flow in Pkd2 ecKO cells was only ~ 11.6 pA or ~50% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells.
source: In contrast, the apamin/tram-34-mediated increase in inward current under flow in Pkd2 ecKO cells was only ~ 11.6 pA or ~50% of that in Pkd2fl/fl cells (Figure 5A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5A,B,D.

claim: In a static bath, apamin/Tram-34 produced a far smaller and similar increase in inward current in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells.
source: In a static bath, apamin/Tram-34 produced a far smaller and similar increase in inward current in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced flow-induced vasodilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries to ~ 77% of that in the control condition.
source: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced both flow- and ACh -induced vasodilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries to ~ 77% and 57% of those that occurred in the control condition (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced ACh-induced vasodilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries to ~ 57% of that in the control condition.
source: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced both flow- and ACh -induced vasodilation in Pkd2fl/fl arteries to ~ 77% and 57% of those that occurred in the control condition (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced mean ACh-induced vasodilation to ~ 54% of that in control in Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: Apamin/Tram-34 reduced mean ACh-induced vasodilation to ~ 54% of that in control in Pkd2 ecKO arteries, which was a similar reduction to that in Pkd2fl/fl arteries (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Apamin/Tram-34 did not alter flow-mediated vasodilation in Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: In contrast, apamin/Tram-34 did not alter flow-mediated vasodilation in Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Bath application of apamin/Tram-34 did not alter the diameter of pressurized, myogenic Pkd2fl/fl or Pkd2 ecKO mesenteric arteries with static intravascular solution.
source: With static intravascular solution, bath application of apamin/Tram-34 did not alter the diameter of pressurized, myogenic Pkd2fl/fl or Pkd2 ecKO mesenteric arteries, indicating that SK and IK channels are not active in the absence of flow or ACh (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2, 5 min, 37°C) increased mean p-eNOS (S1176) protein ~ 1.4 fold in Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: Intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2, 5 min, 37°C) increased mean p-eNOS (S1176) protein ~ 1.4 fold in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, but only ~ 1.08 fold in Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2, 5 min, 37°C) increased mean p-eNOS (S1176) protein only ~ 1.08 fold in Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: Intravascular flow (15 dyn/cm2, 5 min, 37°C) increased mean p-eNOS (S1176) protein ~ 1.4 fold in Pkd2fl/fl arteries, but only ~ 1.08 fold in Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Flow did not alter total eNOS in either Pkd2fl/fl or Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: In contrast, flow did not alter total eNOS in either genotype (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: L-NNA reduced flow-mediated vasodilation to ~ 64% of control in pressurized Pkd2fl/fl arteries.
source: L-NNA, a NOS inhibitor, reduced flow-mediated vasodilation to ~ 64% of control in pressurized Pkd2fl/fl arteries and to ~ 83% of control in Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: L-NNA reduced flow-mediated vasodilation to ~ 83% of control in pressurized Pkd2 ecKO arteries.
source: L-NNA, a NOS inhibitor, reduced flow-mediated vasodilation to ~ 64% of control in pressurized Pkd2fl/fl arteries and to ~ 83% of control in Pkd2 ecKO arteries (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by pressurized artery myography data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Diastolic blood pressure was ~ 9 mmHg higher in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Diastolic and systolic blood pressures were ~ 9 and 14 mmHg higher, respectively, in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice, which translated to a mean arterial pressure (MAP) that was raised by ~ 11% (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by telemetry measurements shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Systolic blood pressure was ~ 14 mmHg higher in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Diastolic and systolic blood pressures were ~ 9 and 14 mmHg higher, respectively, in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice, which translated to a mean arterial pressure (MAP) that was raised by ~ 11% (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by telemetry measurements shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was raised by ~ 11% in Pkd2 ecKO compared to Pkd2fl/fl mice.
source: Diastolic and systolic blood pressures were ~ 9 and 14 mmHg higher, respectively, in Pkd2 ecKO than Pkd2fl/fl mice, which translated to a mean arterial pressure (MAP) that was raised by ~ 11% (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by telemetry measurements shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Locomotion was similar between Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO genotypes.
source: Locomotion was similar between genotypes, indicating that the higher blood pressure in Pkd2 ecKO mice was not due to higher activity (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by locomotion measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cardiac output was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Echocardiography measurements indicated that cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were all similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 8C–F.

claim: Fractional shortening was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Echocardiography measurements indicated that cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were all similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 8C–F.

claim: Ejection fraction was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Echocardiography measurements indicated that cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were all similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 8C–F.

claim: Heart rate was similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Echocardiography measurements indicated that cardiac output, fractional shortening, ejection fraction and heart rate were all similar in Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 8C–F.

claim: Proximal tubule diameter was similar in kidneys of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Proximal tubule diameter and glomerular area were also similar in kidneys of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice, indicating no renal dysfunction (Figure 8G–I).
evidence: This is supported by kidney histology data shown in Figure 8G–I.

claim: Glomerular area was similar in kidneys of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice.
source: Proximal tubule diameter and glomerular area were also similar in kidneys of Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO mice, indicating no renal dysfunction (Figure 8G–I).
evidence: This is supported by kidney histology data shown in Figure 8G–I.

claim: Global knockout of a gene can lead to compensatory expression of other genes that produce contrasting and contradictory results.
source: Global knockout of a gene can lead to compensatory expression of other genes that produce contrasting and contradictory results to those expected from studies on isolated cells and tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of global knockout models, supported by subsequent examples.

claim: Global knockout of TRPM4 increased catecholamine secretion that elevated blood pressure in mice.
source: Global knockout of TRPM4, which is expressed in multiple cell types, including arterial smooth muscle, increased catecholamine secretion that elevated blood pressure in mice (Mathar et al., 2010; Earley et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TRPC6 knockout resulted in upregulation of constitutively active TRPC3 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells that caused vasoconstriction and elevated blood pressure.
source: TRPC6 knockout resulted in upregulation of constitutively active TRPC3 channels in arterial smooth muscle cells that caused vasoconstriction and elevated blood pressure (Dietrich et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Global knockout of TRPV4 channels resulted in either the same or lower blood pressure than controls.
source: Global knockout of TRPV4 channels, which are expressed in both arterial smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells, resulted in either the same or lower blood pressure than controls (Earley et al., 2009; Nishijima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inducible, endothelial cell-specific PKD2 knockout did not alter the expression of PKD1, Piezo1, GPR68, SK3, IK or TRPV4 channels in mesenteric arteries.
source: Here, inducible, endothelial cell-specific PKD2 knockout did not alter the expression of PKD1, Piezo1, GPR68, SK3, IK or TRPV4 channels in mesenteric arteries.
evidence: This is supported by Western blotting data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Flow stimulated plasma membrane Ca2+ influx that activated SK/IK channels, producing a steady-state reduction in inward current in Pkd2fl/fl mouse endothelial cells.
source: Flow stimulated plasma membrane Ca2+ influx that activated SK/IK channels, producing a steady-state reduction in inward current in Pkd2fl/fl mouse endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data showing flow-induced currents and their modulation by Ca2+ removal and SK/IK blockers.

claim: PKD2 knockout reduced both the flow-mediated transient inward current and the steady-state reduction in inward current.
source: PKD2 knockout reduced both the flow-mediated transient inward current and the steady-state reduction in inward current that occurred, in part, due to Ca2+-dependent SK/IK channel activation.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp electrophysiology data comparing Pkd2fl/fl and Pkd2 ecKO cells.

claim: Flow elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration and activated eNOS in a Ca2+/calmodulin–dependent manner.
source: Flow elevated intracellular Ca2+ concentration and activated eNOS in a Ca2+/calmodulin–dependent manner (Fleming, 2010; Michel and Vanhoutte, 2010; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 channels are essential to both flow-mediated Ca2+ influx that activates SK/IK channels and to eNOS activation.
source: Here, we show that PKD2 channels are essential to both flow-mediated Ca2+ influx that activates SK/IK channels and to eNOS activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced flow-mediated SK/IK activation and eNOS phosphorylation in Pkd2 ecKO.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that PKD2 homotetramers are voltage-dependent, outwardly rectifying and primarily permeant to Na+ and K+, with low Ca2+ permeability.
source: Recent evidence suggests that PKD2 homotetramers are voltage-dependent, outwardly rectifying and primarily permeant to Na+ and K+, with low Ca2+ permeability (Shen et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD1 and PKD2 in a 1 to 3 ratio can form a heterotetrameric channel that is far more permeant to Ca2+ than PKD2 homotetramers.
source: PKD1 and PKD2 in a 1 to 3 ratio, respectively, can also form a heterotetrameric channel that is far more permeant to Ca2+ than PKD2 homotetramers (Wang et al., 2019; Su et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 has been proposed to interact with TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC5, TRPC7 and TRPV4 channels.
source: PKD2 has also been proposed to interact with TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC5, TRPC7 and TRPV4 channels, but whether heterotetrameric channel formation occurs between these different proteins in native endothelial cells is poorly understood (Miyagi et al., 2009; Tsiokas et al., 1999; Köttgen et al., 2008; Sutton et al., 2006; Du et al., 2014; Du et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 channel activity is flow-dependent.
source: These results indicate that PKD2 channel activity is flow-dependent and show that PKD2 channels function over a broad range of shear stress to elicit vasodilation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing flow-mediated responses across a range of shear stress values.

claim: PKD2 channels function over a broad range of shear stress to elicit vasodilation.
source: These results indicate that PKD2 channel activity is flow-dependent and show that PKD2 channels function over a broad range of shear stress to elicit vasodilation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing flow-mediated vasodilation across shear stress ranges of 3-35 dyn/cm2.

claim: PKD2 channels do not appear to be inherently flow-sensitive.
source: PKD2 channels do not appear to be inherently flow-sensitive.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the need for potential coupling mechanisms.

claim: Potential mechanisms by which flow stimulates PKD2 channels include coupling to PKD1, regulation by microtubules and/or the actin cytoskeleton, and through interaction with TRPV4 and TRPC1.
source: Potential mechanisms by which flow stimulates PKD2 channels include coupling to PKD1, regulation by microtubules and/or the actin cytoskeleton, and through interaction with TRPV4 and TRPC1 (Du et al., 2014; Li et al., 2006; Hardy and Tsiokas, 2020; Nauli et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PKD2 channel knockout did not abolish flow-mediated current modulation in endothelial cells or vasodilation in pressurized arteries.
source: PKD2 channel knockout did not abolish flow-mediated current modulation in endothelial cells or vasodilation in pressurized arteries, suggesting that PKD2 channel-independent mechanisms also contribute to these responses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing residual flow-mediated responses in Pkd2 ecKO.

claim: Flow activates Piezo1 channels in endothelial cells, leading to vasodilation and a reduction in blood pressure.
source: A previous study demonstrated that flow activates Piezo1 channels in endothelial cells, leading to vasodilation and a reduction in blood pressure (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Endothelial cell Piezo1 does not regulate blood pressure during inactivity, but is activated by an increase in flow during exercise, resulting in arterial depolarization and vasoconstriction.
source: In contrast, another study published that endothelial cell Piezo1 does not regulate blood pressure during inactivity, but is activated by an increase in flow during exercise, resulting in arterial depolarization and vasoconstriction (Rode et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Global knockout of GPR68 reduced flow-mediated vasodilation in third-order mesenteric arteries, but did not alter effects of flow in first- or second-order mesenteric arteries.
source: Global knockout of GPR68, a class A rhodopsin-like G protein-coupled receptor, reduced flow-mediated vasodilation in third-order mesenteric arteries, but did not alter effects of flow in first- or second-order mesenteric arteries where it is not expressed (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Recombinant expression of TRPV4, angiotensin type II, histamine, and bradykinin type two receptors has been shown to not produce flow-mediated responses.
source: Other proposed flow-mediated mechanisms include those via TRPV4, angiotensin type II, histamine, and bradykinin type two receptors, although recombinant expression of these proteins has also been shown to not produce flow-mediated responses (Zhang et al., 2009; Chachisvilis et al., 2006; Mendoza et al., 2010; Ramkhelawon et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flow-mediated signaling mechanisms include the release of ATP, which binds in an autocrine manner to purinergic receptors.
source: Signaling mechanism described include the release of ATP, which binds in an autocrine manner to purinergic receptors, adrenomedullin, acting via cell surface receptors containing CALCRL, and ACh that is released by organic cation transporters and activates muscarinic receptors (Wang et al., 2016; Iring et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flow-mediated signaling mechanisms include adrenomedullin, acting via cell surface receptors containing CALCRL.
source: Signaling mechanism described include the release of ATP, which binds in an autocrine manner to purinergic receptors, adrenomedullin, acting via cell surface receptors containing CALCRL, and ACh that is released by organic cation transporters and activates muscarinic receptors (Wang et al., 2016; Iring et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flow-mediated signaling mechanisms include ACh that is released by organic cation transporters and activates muscarinic receptors.
source: Signaling mechanism described include the release of ATP, which binds in an autocrine manner to purinergic receptors, adrenomedullin, acting via cell surface receptors containing CALCRL, and ACh that is released by organic cation transporters and activates muscarinic receptors (Wang et al., 2016; Iring et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: These flow-mediated pathways can also involve eNOS activation.
source: These pathways can also involve eNOS activation (Wang et al., 2016; Iring et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Muscarinic receptor agonists activate TRPV4 channels, leading to Ca2+ influx.
source: Muscarinic receptor agonists activate TRPV4 channels, leading to Ca2+ influx, and promote endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release, both of which can stimulate SK and IK channels and eNOS to produce vasodilation (Sonkusare et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2010; Fleming and Busse, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Muscarinic receptor agonists promote endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release, which can stimulate SK and IK channels and eNOS to produce vasodilation.
source: Muscarinic receptor agonists activate TRPV4 channels, leading to Ca2+ influx, and promote endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release, both of which can stimulate SK and IK channels and eNOS to produce vasodilation (Sonkusare et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2010; Fleming and Busse, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The relative proportion of muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling pathways differs depending on the arterial bed that is studied.
source: The relative proportion of each of these pathways to muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling differs depending on the arterial bed that is studied.
evidence: This is a general statement about variability in signaling mechanisms across different vascular beds.

claim: PKD2 channel activation stimulates IK/SK channels and eNOS.
source: Here, we show that PKD2 channel activation also stimulates IK/SK channels and eNOS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing flow-mediated activation of these pathways in a PKD2-dependent manner.

claim: IK/SK and eNOS are common downstream targets for both TRPV4 and PKD2 channels.
source: Thus IK/SK and eNOS are common downstream targets for both TRPV4 and PKD2 channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with known TRPV4 signaling.

claim: Flow activates PKD2 channels in endothelial cells via a compartmentalized mechanism that excludes signaling from muscarinic receptors.
source: A reasonable explanation for differential signaling elicited by flow and muscarinic receptors is that flow activates PKD2 channels in endothelial cells via a compartmentalized mechanism that excludes signaling from muscarinic receptors.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed differential signaling.

claim: Homozygous knockout of Pkd2 is lethal in mice.
source: Homozygous knockout of Pkd2 is lethal in mice, precluding study of the global absence of this gene product on vascular function.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Pkd2 knockout mice.

claim: ACh-induced vasodilation was attenuated due to a decrease in the availability of nitric oxide in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2 heterozygous (Pkd2+/-) mice aged between 16 and 20 weeks.
source: ACh-induced vasodilation was attenuated due to a decrease in the availability of nitric oxide in mesenteric arteries of Pkd2 heterozygous (Pkd2+/-) mice aged between 16 and 20 weeks (Brookes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: ADPKD occurs due to mutations in Pkd1 or Pkd2.
source: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) occurs due to mutations in Pkd1 or Pkd2 and is the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide, affecting 1 in 400–1000 individuals (Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: ADPKD is the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide, affecting 1 in 400–1000 individuals.
source: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) occurs due to mutations in Pkd1 or Pkd2 and is the most prevalent monogenic human disease worldwide, affecting 1 in 400–1000 individuals (Torres et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: More than 275 variants in human Pkd2 have been identified.
source: More than 275 variants in human Pkd2 have been identified (http://pkdb.pkdcure.org).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a database.

claim: ADPKD patients can develop hypertension prior to any kidney dysfunction.
source: Although ADPKD is characterized by the appearance of renal cysts, patients can develop hypertension prior to any kidney dysfunction (Torres et al., 2007; Valero et al., 1999; Martinez-Vea et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Short-term endothelial cell PKD2 knockout increased systemic blood pressure without inducing cardiac or renal abnormalities.
source: Here, short-term endothelial cell PKD2 knockout increased systemic blood pressure without inducing cardiac or renal abnormalities.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased blood pressure but normal cardiac function and kidney anatomy in Pkd2 ecKO mice.

claim: ADPKD patients may develop hypertension due to dysfunctional endothelial cell PKD2 channels and attenuated flow-mediated vasodilation.
source: These data suggest that ADPKD patients may develop hypertension due to dysfunctional endothelial cell PKD2 channels and attenuated flow-mediated vasodilation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: During an increase in sustained blood flow, human ADPKD patients display loss of nitric oxide release and an associated reduction in endothelium-dependent dilation in conduit arteries.
source: During an increase in sustained blood flow, human ADPKD patients display loss of nitric oxide release and an associated reduction in endothelium-dependent dilation in conduit arteries, consistent with the results obtained in our mouse model (Lorthioir et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Phosphorylation of bovine eNOS at serine 1179 leads to activation.
source: Phosphorylation of bovine eNOS at serine 1179 and human eNOS at serine 1177 leads to activation (Fulton et al., 1999; Dimmeler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Phosphorylation of human eNOS at serine 1177 leads to activation.
source: Phosphorylation of bovine eNOS at serine 1179 and human eNOS at serine 1177 leads to activation (Fulton et al., 1999; Dimmeler et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
